beats.caption: A CRM built for this demo — the host application
beats.say: Fine-grained access control already exists — a token can be limited to one project, or to read-only. What is harder is temporary delegation at the moment the work happens: a person deciding, right now, that an assistant may touch these records, through these fields, for the next ten minutes. This CRM is the host application; the layer underneath turns that decision into a permission an agent can be held to.

beats.caption: Selection defines a proposed scope. Nothing is granted yet.
beats.say: Here I select two customer records. Nothing has been delegated — selecting something in the interface does not change what an assistant may access. It only defines the scope I am about to offer.

beats.caption: 2 accounts · 2 fields · 10 minutes
beats.say: Now I grant it: these two accounts, only these two fields, for ten minutes, with the countdown starting immediately. That is a mandate.

beats.caption: Human permission → live WebMCP tool
beats.say: The moment I approve it, three things happen. The delegated records are marked. The panel reads the exact scope back to me, so I can check what I allowed. And the permission is compiled into a live WebMCP tool — one that did not exist before the grant, exposing only the records and fields this mandate covers.

beats.caption: Allowed → staged · Outside the mandate → rejected
beats.say: The assistant can now call it. Its first request is inside the mandate, so the server accepts it and stages a change against the record — visible, but not committed. Then it asks for a record that was never delegated, and the call is rejected. Enforcement does not rest on what the tool advertises: every call reaches the server carrying its mandate, and the scope is checked again before anything happens.

beats.caption: The agent can stage. Only the person can apply.
beats.say: There is a second boundary. The assistant can prepare a change but cannot commit one — no apply tool is registered for the agent at all, and the inspector makes that absence explicit. The final action stays with the person who granted the permission.

beats.caption: Production UI: a persistent badge, the decision on the record
beats.say: This panel exists only to explain what is happening; a real user needs none of it. The production interface is a persistent badge while a mandate is live, and an indication on each record of what the agent proposed — a running delegation must never become invisible.

beats.caption: Same delegation layer · Different application
beats.say: The mechanism is not specific to CRM software. This is the same layer inside a deployment console: the resources are services, the permitted properties are replica counts and feature flags. The generated tool changes because it is derived from what the host declares. The delegation model does not.

beats.caption: ChatGPT Desktop · real site tools · real executeTool calls
beats.say: So far this has been the mechanism from inside the application. Here it is from the agent's side: ChatGPT Desktop, using this site's actual WebMCP tools, making real calls against the permission I granted a minute ago. Which is how delegation works between people too. If a colleague covers for me I don't hand over my account — I tell them what they may handle, how far it goes, and when it ends. The decision already exists. A mandate is what turns it into something a machine can enforce.

beats.caption: Human intent → a temporary, enforceable WebMCP capability
beats.say: So: a person defines a temporary scope at the moment it is needed, the system compiles that intent into a live WebMCP contract, and re-validates it on every request. Today I granted that from inside the application. The next step is to move the decision into the agent's own conversation — it asks for the access it needs, the person approves a temporary mandate there, and no broader credential ever changes hands.
